steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on making active learning more cost-efficient on noisy datasets. It should review active learning and uncertainty sampling, the main practical challenges, recent work, our assumptions and approach, and the paper's structure.

- Paper organization

steps.text:
Active learning is a specialized kind of machine learning that tries to optimize the learning process by selecting in an intelligent way the data points that are most beneficial for training the model. Traditional supervised learning uses all the labeled examples that are available, but active learning focuses on using data points where the model is most uncertain, and so it stands to gain the most information. This is especially valuable when labeled data is scarce or expensive to get, for example in medical imaging, natural language processing, or robotics.

Uncertainty sampling was one of the earliest and most influential techniques in active learning. It was first popularized by Lewis, and it showed promise for improving the performance of text classification models. Later Schohn and Cohn expanded the method and applied it to Support Vector Machine (SVM) classification, which made it more established as a strong tool for improving models. Over the years uncertainty sampling has been researched a lot and applied in many domains, and it features prominently in studies by several groups. Much of the work in this area has been empirical or heuristic, but there has also been significant theoretical work, with contributions from other researchers.

Uncertainty sampling is a cornerstone in active learning, but it is not the only strategy that is used. Other approaches like query-by-committee, expected model change, expected error reduction, and expected variance reduction give other ways of implementing active learning effectively. These methods make active learning more adaptable and applicable, so it stays a vibrant field of study. Readers who want a more in-depth understanding of active learning can refer to existing survey papers, and a more recent one.

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Active learning is a specialized kind of machine learning that tries to optimize the learning process by selecting in an intelligent way the data points that are most beneficial for training the model. Traditional supervised learning uses all the labeled examples that are available, but active learning focuses on using data points where the model is most uncertain, and so it stands to gain the most information. This is especially valuable when labeled data is scarce or expensive to get, for example in medical imaging, natural language processing, or robotics.

Uncertainty sampling was one of the earliest and most influential techniques in active learning. It was first popularized by Lewis, and it showed promise for improving the performance of text classification models. Later Schohn and Cohn expanded the method and applied it to Support Vector Machine (SVM) classification, which made it more established as a strong tool for improving models. Over the years uncertainty sampling has been researched a lot and applied in many domains, and it features prominently in studies by several groups. Much of the work in this area has been empirical or heuristic, but there has also been significant theoretical work, with contributions from other researchers.

Uncertainty sampling is a cornerstone in active learning, but it is not the only strategy that is used. Other approaches like query-by-committee, expected model change, expected error reduction, and expected variance reduction give other ways of implementing active learning effectively. These methods make active learning more adaptable and applicable, so it stays a vibrant field of study. Readers who want a more in-depth understanding of active learning can refer to existing survey papers, and a more recent one.

Even though active learning is efficient in sampling, it has several challenges. The first one is the cold start issue: the effectiveness of uncertainty sampling depends heavily on how accurately the initial model captures the overview of the existing data distribution. If the initial model is poorly fitted, both the later queries and the overall model performance are less effective. The second one is that real-world datasets often have noise or features that are not representative enough, and this can make the regions of uncertainty less valuable for querying. The third one is that labeling costs can be different for positive and negative instances; for example, in the financial services industry, identifying a loan/mortgage default is much more costly than identifying a reliable paymaster. For a more complete discussion of the practical challenges of active learning, see that recent survey.

Recent active learning research has made big advances, especially in deep learning. For example, one work addresses the cold start issue in deep learning models by using different querying strategies for high and low budget regimes. Another work assumes that there are plenty of pre-labeled instances, which may contain noise. They use a high-quality model to find and remove dubious or noisy labels, and then go to an oracle for final verification and adjustment.

In this paper we assume the dataset has both labeled and unlabeled data, and no free weakly-labeled data, which is different from what is common in deep learning studies. We assume that overlapping features cause labeling noise in the dataset and make things ambiguous for the classification model. To deal with these issues, we introduce a broader sampling spectrum so that the model does not over-sample noisy regions. We also propose a metric for cost efficiency that takes into account the different labeling costs for positive instances.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows: Section 2 introduces the basic algorithms of random sampling and uncertainty sampling, which are the benchmarks for our method. Section 3 explains our proposed sampling function with mathematical modeling and an algorithm description. Section 4 shows simulation results that compare random sampling, uncertainty sampling, and our proposed sampling function. Section 5 gives the conclusions of our work.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Active learning is a specialized form of machine learning that aims to optimize the learning process by intelligently selecting the data points that are most beneficial for model training [1,2,3]. Unlike traditional supervised learning, which uses all available labeled examples, active learning focuses on data points where the model is most uncertain and hence stands to gain the most information. This approach is especially valuable in scenarios where labeled data is scarce or expensive to obtain, such as medical imaging, natural language processing, or robotics.

Building on this concept, uncertainty sampling emerged as one of the earliest and most influential techniques in active learning. Initially popularized by Lewis [4], this approach showed promise in enhancing the performance of text classification models. The method was later expanded upon by Schohn and Cohn [5], who applied it to Support Vector Machine (SVM) classification, further establishing it as a potent tool for model improvement. Over the years, uncertainty sampling has been extensively researched and applied in various domains, featuring prominently in studies by [6,7,8,9,10]. While much of the work in this area has been empirical or heuristic, there has also been significant theoretical exploration, with contributions from researchers like [11,12].

While uncertainty sampling is a cornerstone of the active learning landscape, it is not the only strategy in use. Other approaches, such as query-by-committee [13], expected model change [14], expected error reduction [15], and expected variance reduction [16], offer alternative ways to implement active learning effectively. These methodologies further extend the adaptability and applicability of active learning, ensuring it remains a vibrant field of study. For a more in-depth understanding of active learning, interested readers can refer to survey papers such as [3,17], and the more recent [18].

Despite its sampling efficiency, active learning presents several challenges. First, there is the cold start issue: the effectiveness of uncertainty sampling relies heavily on how accurately the initial model captures the overview of the existing data distribution, and a poorly fitted initial model reduces the efficacy of both subsequent queries and overall model performance. Second, real-world datasets often contain noise or features that are not adequately representative, making the regions of uncertainty potentially less valuable for querying. Third, labeling costs can vary between positive and negative instances; for instance, in the financial services industry, identifying a loan/mortgage default is substantially more costly than identifying a reliable paymaster. For a more comprehensive discussion of the practical challenges of active learning, refer to [18].

Recent active learning research has made significant advances, particularly in deep learning. For example, [19] addresses the cold start issue in deep learning models by establishing different querying strategies for high and low budget regimes. [20] assumes an abundance of pre-labeled instances, which may contain noise, and employs a high-quality model to identify and remove dubious or noisy labels, turning to an oracle for final verification and adjustment.

In this paper, we assume that the dataset contains both labeled and unlabeled data, with no free weakly-labeled data, unlike what is commonly found in deep learning studies. We assume that overlapping features contribute to labeling noise in the dataset and present ambiguity for the classification model. To address these issues, we introduce a broader sampling spectrum to prevent the model from over-sampling noisy regions. Furthermore, we propose a cost-efficiency metric that considers the distinct labeling costs for positive instances.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 introduces the foundational algorithms of random sampling and uncertainty sampling, which serve as benchmarks for our proposed method. Section 3 describes our proposed sampling function through mathematical modeling and an algorithmic description. Section 4 presents simulation results comparing random sampling, uncertainty sampling, and our proposed sampling function. Finally, Section 5 offers conclusions.
